main_point.en: Jesus endured betrayal for our salvation.

christ_connection.en: Jesus’s teachings about eating His flesh and drinking His blood weren't literal, so they were difficult to understand. Many turned away from Jesus because of these words, but it is in them that we find eternal life made known to us in Jesus’s death and resurrection.

content.en:
17 And when it was evening, he came with the twelve.
18 And as they were reclining at table and eating, Jesus said, “Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me, one who is eating with me.”
19 They began to be sorrowful and to say to him one after another, “Is it I?”
20 He said to them, “It is one of the twelve, one who is dipping bread into the dish with me.
21 For the Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.”

22 And as they were eating, he took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to them, and said, “Take; this is my body.”
23 And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, and they all drank of it.
24 And he said to them, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.
25 Truly, I say to you, I will not drink again of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of God.”
26 And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives.
27 And Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away, for it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.’
28 But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.”
29 Peter said to him, “Even though they all fall away, I will not.”
30 And Jesus said to him, “Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.”
31 But he said emphatically, “If I must die with you, I will not deny you.” And they all said the same.

Leaders: This week, walk with students to help them understand the beautiful significance of the Lord’s Supper and why we partake in it still. Help them understand why we must approach it with reverence and gratitude.

“To break bread with someone was to enter into a pact of friendship and mutual trust. It would be an act of incredible treachery to break bread and then to betray your host. Not only was it someone who was breaking bread with Jesus—but it was one of His own friends who had been with Him for more than two years. This would have seemed unbelievable to the disciples. They did not know that Judas had already made arrangements to betray Jesus.”²⁴

“Even though Judas’s betrayal was ordained according to God’s plan, he is morally responsible for his freewill action. Jesus will be betrayed and crucified according to God’s predetermined will, but this in no way relieved Judas of his responsibility and guilt. In a divine mystery we will never completely comprehend in this life, we embrace the truth and tension that divine sovereignty never cancels out human freedom and moral responsibility. Both are true.”²⁵

“A closer reading of the texts surrounding the Last Supper also reveals many indicators that Jesus’s death should be understood as the focal point. For example, the event is framed and interwoven with the sections about Judas’s betrayal of Jesus. This sets up the reader to be thinking about Jesus’s impending death. Moreover, Matthew, Mark, and John all retell the story of Jesus’s anointing by one ‘Mary’ as part of the buildup to the Passover, and Jesus explicitly comments that this was done in preparation for His burial. Additionally, the Passover week setting of the Supper, with its high point of the atoning, sacrificial lamb, easily pushes our thoughts toward Jesus’s own death as we read the Supper account.”²⁶

All the Gospel writers included this narrative, and it’s a tough passage to wrap our minds around. The disciples had no idea what they were walking into for this last supper with Jesus, and when He shared that one of them would betray Him, they each looked at their own hearts. In the other Gospel writings, Judas was named and sat silently to see what the others would say in response which “showed their innocence, and their attachment to Jesus. It showed how sensitive they were to the least suspicion of the kind.”²⁷ These men had given up everything to follow Jesus, and the idea that one of them had betrayed Him (and the rest of the disciples in turn) was unimaginable. Even though Jesus had been preparing them for these events to happen, they weren’t ready. Peter in particular spoke out, as was in character for him. He decidedly stood firm that he would never betray Jesus, but Jesus knew better. Peter was brash and loved Jesus with such passion that he couldn’t imagine doing what Jesus said he would do. One commentator wrote that “we little know how feeble we are till we are tried.”²⁸ The disciples truly struggled to follow Jesus’s words at the table. Their world had just begun to turn upside down again, and they couldn’t figure out what to do. Though every disciple agreed they’d never betray Jesus, in a few short hours, they would all flee in fear, leaving Jesus alone in His darkest moments.

All true believers endure to the end. Those God has accepted because of Jesus and sanctified by His Spirit will never fall away from the state of grace but will persevere to the end. Believers may fall into sin through neglect and temptation, grieving the Spirit, impairing their graces and comforts, and bringing shame on the cause of Christ and temporary judgments on themselves, yet they will be kept by the power of God through faith for salvation.

Father, give us the same passion that the disciples had, but pair it with the knowledge we have today so we won't betray or deny You. As believers in Christ, You are everything to us. Help us when we are weak so that You can be seen as strong!

question.en: Would you rather a home-cooked meal or takeout (1=Home every time; 10=Give me takeout daily)?

instructions.en:
These optional activities are designed to help your students interact. You’ll find a Discussion Activity and a Cultural Connection, which touches on a relevant topic in today’s teen culture. Each group is different, so adapt these activities to fit your group’s needs. The goal is for students to connect more to the lesson as they connect to the topic and to one another.

Ask the following questions, allowing time for students to share responses:

question.en: What does it mean to lose trust in someone?
Share about a time when you were confident you wouldn't make a mistake and then you did. How did you react to messing up?
Have you ever been hurt or betrayed by someone you care about?

content.en: Trust is hard to gain and easy to lose. One of the worst feelings is knowing that you’ve disappointed someone so much that you lost their trust. Being a person who is trustworthy and dependable is what makes a great friend, but living it out isn’t always easy.

cultural_connection.en: Let’s talk about trust. Can you really be trusted? If you made a list of the most important qualities you want in a friend, trust is probably on your list. Finding friends who are trustworthy is crucial in a culture where betrayal can happen on social media in an instant, but we must be trustworthy too—especially if we claim to love Jesus. If you’ve ever had a friend or family member betray your trust, you know how much it hurts. The sting of betrayal lasts a long time and isn’t repaired easily—sometimes, not at all. How you handle betrayal says a lot about who you are and what you believe. If you run to the nearest person who will listen to gossip and complain, then you’re reacting more like the world. Jesus showed us a better way. The amazing truth is that God will never betray you; He is perfectly trustworthy. We learn from Him what trust looks like! Though we may have great friends, Jesus is our greatest Friend. The more you depend on Him, the more you realize He is the only One capable of never letting you down.

question.en: How could Jesus casually bring up someone betraying Him?

answer.en: Jesus knew exactly what was happening and trusted God throughout the process. Jesus knew He came for this moment. The disciples were in the middle of eating a meal with Jesus when He dropped a bombshell of information that would forever change the course of their lives and their ministries. If we knew the betrayal Judas had committed, we likely would’ve retaliated in some way. But Jesus placed His trust in the Father, not in anyone or in anything of this world. Jesus so trusted the Lord that He could endure the worst betrayal.

question.en: How did the disciples respond to what Jesus shared?

answer.en: Have you ever racked your brain to recall if you’ve done something wrong? The disciples did this—panicking that maybe they had messed up somewhere. We can imagine the tension in the room. Jesus’s friends couldn’t imagine intentionally betraying Him and felt distressed at the very thought. Each of them tried to talk it out with Jesus and probably combed over in their minds every conversation and interaction to try and remember if they had done anything like what Jesus mentioned. The disciples’ love for Jesus made them feel like betraying Jesus was impossible, but one of them did. And soon, they all would to some degree.

question.en: Read John 13:1-5. If Jesus knew He would be betrayed by Judas, why did He still let Judas be so close to Him and do ministry with Him?

answer.en: We struggle to understand God’s sovereignty—in other words, God’s complete authority over all things. He can see what we can’t see and knows all. He is always on time and is intentional about getting glory, so we choose to trust that His plan is good, even if it doesn’t make sense to us. Jesus still faithfully taught Judas, utilized his gifts and skills, and was a brother and friend to him, even though He knew Judas would betray Him. Let’s also remember that though Jesus was God in flesh, He was also fully human. He wasn’t immune to the sting of His friend’s betrayal, but Jesus knew there was purpose, even in betrayal. It would serve as a part of the process and move the timeline along toward the cross. Jesus trusted in God’s ultimate plan, even though the process was painful in every way. He treated His betrayer with compassion and dignity, even washing his feet along with the others (John 13:2-5). What an example for us to follow!

question.en: What did Jesus mean by saying we’re supposed to eat His body and drink His blood?

answer.en: Jesus’s instructions were deeply symbolic, first for His disciples and now for us. The acts of breaking bread and pouring a drink remind us of Jesus’s sacrifice for our sins. As a community, Christians are supposed to take the Lord’s Supper regularly (also called Communion). The broken bread pointed back to the manna God provided in the wilderness (Deut. 8:3). Jesus was born in Bethlehem, which means “house of bread,” and called Himself the “bread of life” (John 6:35).²⁹ His body was literally broken for us. The drink pointed to the blood spilled by countless animal sacrifices and to the final sacrifice Jesus made when He spilled His blood for us. Paul gave instructions about the Lord’s Supper, reminding us, “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Cor. 11:23-26).

question.en: Why was Jesus committed to sacrificing Himself?

answer.en: Old Testament prophecies pointed to the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus. In this passage, Jesus quoted Zechariah 13:7, explaining that He was the Shepherd who was about to be struck down in death, and even His closest followers would run (v. 27). He was committed to obeying the Father and to fulfilling these prophecies because He saw the bigger picture—He was born to save us from sin; even His name meant this (Matt. 1:21)! Jesus did the will of His Father, no matter the cost to Himself, because of His love for the Father and for us.

question.en: How can the way we live deny that we know Jesus? What can we do when we fall?

answer.en: If we’re honest, answering this question is tough. Even Jesus’s closest friends denied Him and ran in fear when the pressure hit. We’re prone to the same fears, so we can’t say we’d do things differently. We can deny Jesus in the way we speak and act, in remaining silent or in not loving others. Living in a way that reflects we know Jesus is a daily, active choice. The capacity to betray Him lives inside each of us. No one is perfect or immune to sin. Peter was convinced he would never do this, but Jesus knew better. If Peter and the disciples can fall for a moment, so can we. If we fall, we don’t have to stay there; we can get up, repent, and love Jesus and others. We can get in the Word and ask people to hold us accountable.

question.en: Who do you have in place to hold you accountable so that you are guarded from falling away or denying Jesus?

answer.en: Nothing guarantees you'll never slip up, but you can take wise steps to remain close to the Lord. Your time spent in the Bible is never wasted, and spending time with other believers is necessary to sharpen your faith (Prov. 27:17). If you don’t have people to hold you accountable, pray for God to send someone. While you wait, look for someone else who needs a solid Christian friend and be that friend! The world will often say that you should spend your younger years living it up and being free, but you're never too young to walk closely with Jesus and let your passion for Him drive everything you do; that is real freedom. You don’t have to buy into the lie that you can wait until you're older. Ask God to show you how to live more intentionally—in a way that holds you accountable and encourages others. Instead of trying to do things on your own or pridefully thinking you’ll never fall (that didn’t work out well for the disciples, did it?), link arms with other believers. You'll find strength to stand when doing so is costly.

content.en:
In school, it feels like everything has a barrier to entry. Want to be in the Honors Society? You need the GPA. Want to play varsity? You need the skill. Want to sit at “that” table? You need the right clothes, the right personality, or the right last name. These groups are exclusive because they are designed to keep people out based on qualifications. If you don’t check the boxes, you don’t get in.

Christianity is also exclusive but for a completely different reason. It’s not exclusive because of who gets in—it’s exclusive because of how we get in. In John 14, the disciples were spiraling. Jesus was talking about leaving, and they were confused and anxious. Thomas, being the honest one in the group, basically said, “Lord, we have no idea where you're going, so how can we know the way?” Jesus’s response changed everything: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” Here is the shift: Most exclusive clubs invite a select few but offer many ways to fail. Jesus invites everyone (John 7:37) but offers only one way to succeed. He is the Way, the path itself. He is the Truth, the ultimate reality. And He is the Life, the source of meaningful, full life we are all searching for.

When Philip asked Jesus to “show us the Father,” Jesus said: “I am in the Father and the Father is in me.” By using the phrase “I Am,” Jesus used the ancient, holy name of God (Yahweh) that was revealed to Moses. He was telling the disciples—and us—that He isn’t just a good teacher or a life coach. He is God in the flesh. He has the authority to promise us a place in heaven because it’s His throne room. You don’t have to be wealthy, good enough, or from the right family to belong to God. The invitation is open to all, but the entrance is singular. We don’t get to the Father by being a better version of ourselves; we get to Him by trusting the One who is the Way.

question.en: How does it feel to know God’s requirement isn’t based on your performance, GPA, or popularity?
Jesus says He is the way, not just a way. What is the difference, and why is it so important?

prayer.en: Jesus, You are the Way, the Truth, and the Life. Thank You for making a pathway to eternal life with You. Help me walk worthy of Your gift of salvation.

content.en:
Jesus was preparing His disciples for His departure, but He promised they wouldn't be alone. He was sending help. Why? Because He loved them. And those who love Him show it by keeping His commands. We don’t obey Jesus to get His love; we already have it. We obey Jesus to show Him that we love Him in return.

You might want to be obedient, but you ask, “How will I know if I’m being obedient or disobedient?” Two things help you obey: (1) Knowing God’s Word. If you know it, you'll know when you stray from it. (2) Seeking His help—the Helper, actually! Jesus promised that when He left the disciples, He would send the Holy Spirit as a Counselor. He will teach and remind His followers of His commands.

The Holy Spirit fills a lot of roles: Counselor, Helper, Comforter, Advocate, Spirit of Truth, Spirit of God, and more. The Greek word here is paraclete, which means to come alongside. Jesus was sending the disciples (and us) someone to walk alongside them, just as He had, to continue to teach them and remind them of what Jesus had already taught them. He does this for us too. If you are a follower of Jesus Christ, the Holy Spirit doesn’t just walk alongside you, but He lives in you and works daily to teach and remind you of Jesus’s commands.

If you don’t recognize the Spirit’s work in your life, you may want to take a step back and ask yourself some honest questions: Have I truly made Jesus the Lord of my life? Have I surrendered to His will for me? Am I listening? Am I ignoring the teaching and leading of the Holy Spirit? The Holy Spirit’s job is to come alongside us in our sanctification—a lifelong process where we grow more and more like Jesus. He teaches us and reminds us of the commands we’ve been given. In return, we listen and follow the commands. Why? Because obedience is the evidence of a faith-filled love for Jesus. If we love Him, we obey Him.

question.en: When have you sensed the Holy Spirit working in your life?
How can your obedience be evidence of your love for Jesus?

prayer.en: Jesus, thank You for sending me the Holy Spirit, who works in my life, daily teaching me to be more like You. Help me grow and learn from Him always.

content.en:
In our world, most “love” is conditional—based on how you look, how you perform, or what you can do for someone else. But in John 15:9-17, Jesus described a kind of love that is completely different. It doesn’t start with you; it starts with the Father, flows through Jesus, and ends up in your heart.

Jesus started by saying, “Abide in my love.” To remain means to make your home there, to stay, to abide. Imagine your phone—it only works if it’s charged. If left unplugged, it eventually dies. Staying connected to Jesus through prayer, His Word, and worship is how we stay “charged” with His love. We don’t have to manufacture kindness or patience on our own; we just have to stay plugged into the Source.

This is one of the most mind-blowing shifts in the Bible. Jesus told His disciples—and us—that He no longer called them servants, but friends. Servants just do what they’re told without knowing the “why.” A friend is brought into the inner circle. Jesus has shared His heart, His mission, and His life with you. You are a personal friend of the Creator of the universe.

Jesus gives a specific instruction: “Love one another as I have loved you.” How did He love us? Sacrificially. He laid down His life. As Jesus’s friend, you might not die on a cross, but it might mean laying down your pride to apologize first, laying down your time to help a struggling friend, or laying down your reputation to stand up for someone being bullied.

question.en: How can you remain in Jesus this week? What can you do to stay ‘plugged in’ to the Source?
What is one thing you can lay down this week (like your phone, your time, or your ego) to show someone the love of Christ?

prayer.en: Jesus, help me to remain in You, to stay plugged in to You. I want to love others in a way that brings You glory and honor—in the way that You love me.

content.en:
We often see Jesus as the calm, collected hero who has every answer. But in today’s passage, we see a side of Him that is raw, overwhelmed, and deeply relatable. In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus told His friends that He was “very sorrowful, even to death.” Jesus didn’t just say a polite, one-sentence prayer and move on. He fell to the ground and begged God for another way. Mark wrote that He went back three separate times to ask God for another way. He used the word Abba—an intimate, childlike term for “Daddy”—while asking for the “cup” of suffering to be taken away. Don’t miss this: Jesus begged for another way.

If you’ve ever prayed the same prayer over and over, crying until you ran out of words, Jesus has been there. He understands the desperation of wanting a different outcome. God can handle your honesty. You don’t have to “clean up” your prayers or pretend you’re okay with a hard situation. Repetition isn’t a lack of faith. Jesus asked three times. You can keep knocking on heaven’s door when your heart is heavy.

The most powerful part of Jesus’s prayer is the pivot: “Yet not what I will, but what you will.” Even in His agony, Jesus trusted that the Father’s plan was bigger than His temporary pain. God’s will was for the Son to suffer, and Jesus surrendered obediently to His will.

Following Jesus doesn’t mean we always get what we ask for. It means we have a Savior who knows exactly how it feels to hurt, who advocates for us when we’re desperate, and who gives us the strength to trust God’s will—even when it differs from our own desires.

question.en: When have you called out to God with a ‘very sorrowful’ heart?
How does today’s passage bring you comfort in difficult moments?

prayer.en: Jesus, You get it. You know the pain I’ve felt, but I choose to trust Your will. I choose to trust that Your plan is bigger than my temporary pain.

content.en:
Life is full of “ride or die” friendships—until things actually get messy. We all like to think we’d be the one friend who stays when everyone else runs, but today’s passage gives us a brutal reality check on loyalty. Jesus was in the garden, physically and emotionally exhausted, when Judas showed up with a literal mob. Imagine the scene: torches flickering, swords drawn, and the tension at a breaking point. Then comes the “signal.” Judas uses a kiss—the ultimate sign of affection and deep friendship—to identify Jesus for arrest. It’s the ultimate “fake friend” move. Judas wasn’t just a bystander; he was an insider using his intimacy with Jesus as a weapon. In the panic, one of the disciples swings a sword, cutting off an ear. It’s a gut-reaction move: fight. But Jesus shut it down immediately. He pointed out the irony: They had come after Him like He was a dangerous criminal, yet He sat teaching in the temple every day in plain sight.

Jesus wasn’t surprised. He knew this wasn’t an accident or a lapse in security; it was the fulfillment of Scripture. He stayed in total control, even as He surrendered His freedom. Then comes the most horrific moment in the passage: “And they all left him and fled.” Just hours earlier, these guys promised they would die for Jesus. But when the swords came out and the “VIP” status of being a disciple turned into a “Most Wanted” status, they checked out. They chose safety over Savior.

We often judge the disciples, but we do the same thing. We’re “with” Jesus when it’s cool, when the worship music is loud, or when life is easy. But what happens when following Him makes us look “weird” or costs us a social connection? Jesus knew He would walk the road to the cross alone. He could have stopped it all, but He didn’t because the cost was worth it to Him. Our eternal lives were worth it to Him.

question.en: Why do you think it’s easier to fight (like the disciple) than to trust (like Jesus)?
The disciples ran because they were afraid. How has fear made you want to ‘flee’ from your faith?

prayer.en: Lord, forgive me when my loyalty to You is weak. Thank You for being more faithful to me than I could ever be to You.
